title: Batching sensitivity cookbook and load scripts
body:
Purpose:
This is a focused cookbook for diagnosing how batching decisions (batch size, microbatching, pad/truncation policies) affect throughput, latency tails, and GPU occupancy for our serving runtime. It complements higher-level benchmarking playbooks by giving engineers a compact set of experiments and runnable loadgen snippets to pinpoint batching sensitivity without redoing a full benchmark matrix.

Why this matters (notes):
- Small changes in request composition or batching heuristics can flip effective throughput by 10–50% on GPU-bound models.
- Observed failure modes: queue saturation causing long tails, KV-cache pressure increasing latency variance, and oscillations when autoscaler cold-adds workers.
- Need repeatable micro-experiments that isolate batching variables.

Quick checklist before running any experiment:
- Lock model version and quantization profile. Record model id and commit.
- Ensure GPU clock and power profile are stable (use node-level preset).
- Pin network path (same region, avoid crossAZ egress) and disable bursting autoscaler or set very high cooldown.
- Capture perf counters (nvprof / Nsight perf summary) and runtime traces (span id injection) in parallel.
- Use deterministic RNG seeds for synthetic prompts; keep seed in filename.

Core experiments (stepwise):
1) Baseline single-request profile
- Objective: measure single-request latency and token-production cost on cold path and warmed path.
- Config: concurrency=1, sequence_len=64 prompt, token_gen_target=32
- Expected: baseline p50/p95/p99, GPU occupancy ~30–40% for small models, higher for bigger models.

2) Batching ramp (fixed request size)
- Objective: find effective batch size knee for throughput and latency tradeoff.
- Sweep: batch_size = [1,2,4,8,16,32,64] with constant concurrency per client such that offered load covers potential throughput.
- Measurement window: 300s, discard first 60s warmup.
- Metrics: tokens/s (system), p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU SM utilization, CUDA memory alloc/dma rates.
- When to stop increasing batch: diminishing returns in tokens/s (<3% uplift) or p99 latency exceeding SLA.

3) Microbatching (inference-engine internal)
- Objective: understand how sub-batching inside kernels affects latency variance.
- Setup: enable/disable microbatching flag in runtime; for each, run batch sizes [8,16,32].
- Watch: kernel launch counts and sync points; microbatching often reduces p99 but increases p50 if poorly aligned.

4) Sequence-length mixture sensitivity
- Objective: realistic distribution effect.
- Mixes: uniform short(8)/medium(64)/long(512) in ratios [90/9/1, 70/25/5, 40/40/20].
- Note: batch packing heuristics matter — test both pack-by-token and pack-by-request modes.

5) KV cache pressure test (long-context heavy caching)
- Objective: detect throughput degradation when KV caches grow.
- Config: emulate continuing conversations with average sequence per session 1024 tokens; run for 1h to let caches grow.
- Alert: observe GC pauses, increased p99, and memory spikes.

6) Padding vs. dynamic shapes
- Objective: quantify cost of padding to max_len vs. dynamic kernel paths.
- Compare: pad_to_multiple_of=64 vs dynamic.
- Expectation: padding helps throughput for very small models when it reduces kernel branching; hurts for long-tail sequences.

Load generator examples (YAML-style snippet to copy/paste into runner):

# loadgen config: batching sweep sample
loadgen:
  name: batching-sweep-2025-01
  model: redwood/gpt-3x-like:2025-01-06
  clients: 4
  duration_s: 300
  warmup_s: 60
  request_template: |
    {\n      "prompt": "Summarize: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. Seed={seed}",\n      "max_new_tokens": 32\n    }
  sequence_policy: fixed
  sequence_len: 64
  batch_sizes: [1,2,4,8,16,32]
  concurrency_per_client: 8
  rng_seed: 1729
  metrics_output: /tmp/bench-results/batching-1729.csv

# small script to run a single config (bash pseudo)
# ./bin/loadtest --config path/to/config.yaml --output results.json

Repeatability and seed hygiene:
- Always include an explicit rng_seed in the yaml and embed it in the output filename.
- Repeat each point in sweep at least 3 times in separate runs, with 5–10 minute cool-downs between runs to allow cgroups/gpu memory fragmentation to settle.
- Compare runs by steady-window mean (last 200s of a 300s run) and compute coefficient of variation (CoV). Target CoV < 3% for throughput to be considered repeatable for production tuning.

Warmup heuristics (practical):
- Warmup should exercise all code paths that are common. For LLMs: run a brief priming stream of mixed-length requests for 60s then start measurement.
- For batch-sensitive tests: include a repeat of maximal batch-size request to ensure kernel specialization warms.
- If using caching, warmup must also populate KV caches to steady-size.

Observability checklist (what to capture):
- loadgen event logs (request ids, batch ids, timings)
- runtime traces with batch composition (request lengths), kernel names, and microbatch counts
- GPU metrics: SM util, memory utilization, PCIe bandwidth, GPU temperature
- Host metrics: scheduler run-queue, context-switch rate, network queues
- Runtime counters: queued_requests, dropped_requests, batching_latency_ms

Common failure modes and remediation notes:
- Symptom: throughput fluctuates by >10% across identical runs.
  - Check: node-level thermal throttling, non-deterministic autoscaler actions, background cron jobs, or noisy neighbors on shared GPUs.
  - Fix: isolate on dedicated instance or use dedicated capacity and rerun.

- Symptom: p99 latency spikes after long run
  - Check: GC/allocator fragmentation; KV-cache eviction behavior; memory compaction events.
  - Fix: increase periodic compaction interval, cap per-session KV size, or rotate processes.

- Symptom: throughput lower than expected when batch_size high
  - Check: insufficient concurrent outstanding requests to fill batches; client-side pacing limits; serialization overhead per-request.
  - Fix: increase concurrency_per_client, reduce per-request prep work, or enable request coalescing.

Experiment naming convention (important for later analysis):
- {model}-{date}-{batchPolicy}-{batchSize}-{seed}-{runIdx}
- Example: gpt3x-20250110-tokenpack-b32-s1729-r1

Data analysis tips (quick):
- Always align traces by measurement window start. Discard warmup region.
- Aggregate tokens/s across processes rather than simple mean of means.
- Use sliding-window median filter (30s) to locate stable plateau before computing steady-state metrics.

Next steps and suggested follow-ups:
- Add a param sweep for pad_to_multiple_of and microbatching thresholds in the bench harness.
- Create a small dashboard that cross-plots batch_size vs p95 vs SM_util to quickly identify knees.
- Run the same matrix across quantization profiles to find interaction effects.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add example Jupyter notebook for post-run analysis (parse runner CSVs, compute CoV, plot occupancy vs latency).
- Share this cookbook with solutions-eng and include two representative customer workloads as templates.

Relevant links and bookmarks:
- Perf guide: confluence:perf/batching-guides
- Bench repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/benchmarks
- Related ticket: JIRA-INF-4321 (batching regressions triage)

Appendix: short-run troubleshooting commands (examples)
- nvtop / nvidia-smi dmon 1  - watch GPU util in real time
- sudo perf stat -e context-switches,cpu-migrations -p <pid>  - check host contention
- curl -sS http://localhost:8080/metrics | grep batch  - runtime batch counters

End of document.
